Then she heard her own voice say, "First, the ambulance." She dialled 108 and gave the village name and the landmark, the Hanuman temple. Her mother held her father's hand. Only after the call did Disha ask her neighbour Noor to phone her brother. Money and the rest could wait. The ambulance came in twenty minutes.

passage: In the college gym, Tushar, twenty-three, slipped off a treadmill and cut his chin on the rail. Blood dripped onto his shirt, and people stared. He felt dizzy and deeply embarrassed. "I'm fine, I'm fine," he kept saying. Bhavna, the gym instructor, knelt beside him. She didn't say, "Don't worry, it's nothing." Instead she said, "Tushar, you've cut your chin. I'm pressing this towel on it. The college nurse is coming; she'll be here in five minutes. You're going to stay sitting down." Each plain sentence settled him. His breathing slowed. When the nurse arrived, Bhavna told her exactly what had happened, and Tushar felt, for the first time, that he could stop pretending.

Dear Rehana,

I've been meaning to thank you properly for the night I fainted at the bus stop. I don't remember much, but I remember your voice.

I woke up on the pavement feeling ashamed and scared, with strangers staring. You didn't tell me everything was fine. You said, "Chandrika, you fainted. You're lying on the pavement. I've called an ambulance; it's ten minutes away. I'm staying here." And every few minutes, you told me what was happening next.

It sounds small. But it was the first thing that stopped me shaking. Knowing was better than being soothed.

With gratitude,
Chandrika

qa.a: Ten minutes away.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel on waking up on the pavement?
qa.a: Chandrika felt ashamed and scared, with strangers staring.

qa.a: Rehana gave clear, simple statements of what had happened and what was coming next, which calmed Chandrika more than empty reassurance.

Being told the truth was the kindest thing anyone did that day.

Class teacher's note, Class 3, Wednesday.
At lunch break today, Anjali climbed the boundary wall behind the water tank to fetch a ball. The wall is about two metres high and has broken glass on top. When I called her down, she was surprised. "But I didn't fall," she said. She truly had not imagined what could happen. Her friend Omkar was already putting one foot on the wall to follow her. I brought both down, showed them the glass, and explained the rule: balls over the wall are fetched by the peon, never by children. I have asked the office to fix a net there and will remind the class tomorrow.

Today I got in big trouble. Me and my cousin were playing near the main road, and our cricket ball rolled across. I just ran after it. A scooter honked really loud and swerved. Farida aunty from next door screamed and grabbed my arm and pulled me back. She was shaking. I didn't even think about the scooter. I was only thinking about the ball.
Aunty told Ammi, and Ammi made a new rule: if the ball goes on the road, we leave it and call a grown-up. I said that's not fair. But at night I kept thinking about the honk and my tummy felt funny.
Vaibhav

His older brother Ujjwal, fifteen, came round the corner, saw the smoke and stamped out the straw, then poured a bucket of water over it. Nilesh stood frozen. "I only wanted to see," he whispered. Ujjwal took the matches and called their father. That evening, Papa put the matchbox on a high shelf and made a rule: no fire without a grown-up, ever.

passage: The monsoon had turned the ghat road outside Mahabaleshwar slick, and Bhupen, fifteen, knew it. His friends had their phones out. "No hands down the slope, Bhupen! You said you could!" Ishita, his neighbour, said quietly, "It's wet. Don't." But everyone was watching, and backing out felt worse than falling. He pushed off, lifted his hands and grinned for the cameras. Ishita ran to him, then called his mother, who came with the car and took him to the clinic. That night, he deleted the group's video himself.

passage: On the terrace of their Mumbai building, Suraj, sixteen, and four friends were making videos. Deepak said, "Stand on the water-tank ledge and do a pose. Ten seconds. The switchboard in my kitchen has had a loose wire hanging out for two months. I've been turning on the kettle around it every morning without thinking. Usha aunty, my landlady, said she'd call the electrician. She didn't, and I stopped asking because nothing ever happened.

Tomorrow morning: I'm calling an electrician myself and telling Usha aunty I'll share the bill. Not waiting any more.
Kashish

Tuesday. She photographed the gaps, measured them and wrote a short note: "East scaffold, level 3: two braces missing. Risk of collapse. Suggest: stop work there until replaced; spare braces in store room B." She handed it to her supervisor, Harish, and said it plainly.
Wednesday. Harish replied, "We're behind schedule." Irawati said, "I know. It's four hours of work to fix. A fall would stop the site for weeks." He paused, then sent two workers to fit the braces. Work resumed that afternoon.

passage: Kunal, you've just started at the chemical plant, so listen to your Bua, Kashish. When I was twenty-five, I worked in a paint factory in Vapi. One day my manager told me to mix two solvents in the open room instead of under the hood, because the hood fan was broken and we were rushing. My hands went cold. I said, "Sir, the label says these fumes are harmful in a closed room. The fan in room two is working. Can we move the batch there? It's a ten-minute walk." He shouted a little. I stayed calm and repeated the facts. He agreed. That year, another factory had people hospitalised doing exactly what he'd asked.

Today Sahil, five, asked if he could set out the plates for snack time. He carried them one by one from the shelf, very seriously, tongue between his teeth. It took him nearly ten minutes, twice as long as usual. One plate went on the floor; he picked it up and put it back on the table, and I swapped it for a clean one without fuss. When everyone sat down, he announced, "I did the plates!" and beamed. I thanked him in front of the class. I will give him the same job all this week, and let him choose a helper on Friday.
Vinita

passage: In their village near Mysuru, Devika, four, followed her grandfather Harsha to the cowshed every morning. Today she wanted to carry the small bucket of water. Dada swept it again later without a word. At breakfast, Devika told Amma, "I fed the cow," puffing her chest out.

passage: At the residential school in the hills, new students in Class 4 had to learn three things in the first week: pack their own bag each night, make their bed before assembly and make tea in the hostel kitchen under the warden's eye. It was too sweet, but everyone drank it. Jaya wrote home: "Amma, how do you do all this every day?"
